body: Tuesday, September 01 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed under Chair Warsh is in a hawkish posture, with markets now pricing a potential rate hike in September. The 10Y yield surged to 4.79% (+16 bps vs 4W ago), the 2Y at 4.34% (prior close, +9 bps vs 4W), with the 10Y-2Y spread at +41 bps — positively sloped but still flat by historical standards — as the whole curve reprices higher on inflation re-acceleration fears. The fiscal backdrop remains expansive — Goldman Sachs CEO publicly stated America must either "grow faster or spend less." Oil at $89.56 (↑18.2% vs 4W ago) is the accelerant pouring fuel on the inflation fire.

New / Most Important: The bond selloff intensified this week — headlines confirm "rising bond yields and oil prices weigh on stocks" as the S&P 500 dropped to 7632 (↓1.3%) and the Russell 2000 fell harder (↓3.7%), confirming narrow market leadership. Treasury Secretary Bessent met with BOJ's Ueda, calling for "sound policy to avoid currency volatility" — this is the US explicitly outsourcing dollar management to Japan. Markets now see Warsh endorsing a rate hike in September, a seismic shift from any residual easing expectations. The Iran conflict, now six months in, is described as exacting an "uneven economic toll" — investors prospering while consumers pay. Barron's declared "higher Treasury yields are here to stay."

Playbook ✓: Rising oil → rising yields → equity multiple compression is textbook. Mega-cap dominance (Russell/Nasdaq ratio ↓1.6%) is the classic late-cycle flight to quality.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: VIX at 15.93 in COMPLACENCY territory while equities sell off and yields surge is the divergence that matters most. This is structurally dangerous — it suggests hedging demand has been crushed by months of range-trading and vol-selling, yet the macro regime is shifting toward genuine stagflationary risk. The Iran war driving oil +18% in a month should have VIX in the mid-20s at minimum. The gap between realized macro volatility and implied equity volatility is a setup for a violent repricing. Warsh potentially hiking into a war-driven supply shock would be the first Fed rate increase during an active military conflict in decades. The combination of fiscal deficits, war-premium oil, and a hawkish Fed is a capital flow regime the US hasn't navigated since the early 1980s.

Macro Stance: The ECB faces a hawkish inflection point. Eurozone inflation rose to 3.3% in August — a near three-year high — driven by higher energy prices, cementing expectations for a rate hike at the upcoming September meeting. Lending growth picked up per ECB data released last week, suggesting monetary tightening hasn't yet dampened credit demand.

New / Most Important: The August inflation print at 3.3% crossed above the critical 3% threshold, a psychological and policy-significant level that changes the ECB conversation from "hold" to "hike." Multiple sources confirmed this data today. Energy pass-through from the Iran conflict is the proximate cause — this is imported inflation, not demand-driven, yet the ECB appears set to respond with tighter policy. Commerzbank described a "proactive ECB" as supportive for EUR. This is the euro area re-entering a tightening cycle precisely when the growth outlook is deteriorating — a policy error risk that mirrors the ECB's 2011 mistake under Trichet. The global bond selloff is synchronized: US, Europe, Japan all repricing higher simultaneously, draining liquidity from risk assets worldwide. Cross-border capital implications are severe — European credit spreads should widen as the ECB hikes into a supply shock.

Playbook ✓: Oil-driven inflation → ECB hawkishness → EUR strength is the standard response function.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Hiking into a supply shock with no domestic demand overshoot is a potential policy error of historic proportions. The ECB may be fighting the wrong inflation.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is now openly leaning against yuan strength: China is reining in the rising yuan as weak domestic demand clouds the outlook (Reuters, [Aug 31]), with the reference rate set at 6.7828 against an estimate of 6.7344 (investingLive, [Aug 30]) after the currency reached a three-year high (UA.NEWS, [Aug 27]). Liquidity stays ample, with overnight reverse repos resumed ahead of month-end (Gulf Times, [Aug 29]). July CPI slowed to 0.5%, more than expected (BigGo Finance, [Aug 9]), and PPI growth to 3.5%, missing expectations (BigGo Finance, [Aug 8]): price pressure is too weak to justify a strong currency, which is exactly the PBOC's argument.

PMIs & Activity: The two August factory surveys disagree on the level but agree on direction. The official manufacturing PMI rebounded to 49.8 with the new orders index back in expansion (BigGo Finance, [Aug 30]), contracting less than expected (CNBC, [Aug 30]) after July's 49.2 (FXStreet, [Jul 31]); the private manufacturing PMI rose to 51.5, its longest expansion streak in five years (BigGo Finance, [Aug 31]). Reconciled: the private survey leans toward export-oriented firms and is in expansion, while the official gauge stays below 50 because domestic activity is still contracting — the factory rebound remains dependent on exports (EU Today, [Aug 31]) and weak services signal an uneven recovery (Reuters, [Aug 30]). Industrial profits rose 17.6% in January-July (Fibre2Fashion, [Aug 29]) with growth at a seven-month low (Anadolu Ajansı, [Aug 27]), and auto sales slumped 22% (GlobalChinaEV, [Aug 27]).

Credit Impulse: July bank loans posted a record contraction as credit demand faltered (Reuters, [Aug 14]), yet credit growth exceeded forecasts despite the rare loan slump (Bloomberg, [Aug 14]); reconciled, government bonds carry the aggregate while the loan book shrinks, and that leg is about to strengthen as China speeds up bond issuance after a national meeting on investment (South China Morning Post, [Aug 31]). Lenders are thriving regardless: the largest five banks reported their strongest first-half profit since the height of the property crash (Reuters, [Aug 28]) and bank stocks surged on strong earnings (BigGo Finance, [Aug 30]). Beijing is ramping up credit support in its overhaul of the property market (The Business Times, [Aug 29]), the most direct attempt yet to restart household borrowing.

Property: New home prices were stagnant in July as demand stayed weak (Reuters, [Aug 17]). The policy response is structural: China moved to curb housing presales to shore up confidence (Reuters, [Aug 28]), raised the presale threshold under a new national standard (Caixin Global, [Aug 29]) and extended mortgage terms to 40 years (www.briefasia.com, [Aug 30]). The equity verdict has hardened: after a limit-up surge on the mortgage change, property stocks fell as the new rules upend the presale funding playbook (Reuters, [Aug 31]) — a double-edged sword, in the SCMP's phrase (South China Morning Post, [Aug 31]), positive for buyers and negative for developer cash flow. Vanke's first-half loss widened as sales slumped (Caixin Global, [Aug 29]) and a Reuters poll sees the investment slump deepening (Reuters, [Aug 27]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The G20 the US is hosting has turned into a forum on China's surplus: Bessent says G20 countries should consider more trade barriers on China to cut imbalances (Reuters, [Aug 31]) and presses them to confront its $1.2 trillion trade surplus (investingLive, [Aug 30]); Beijing replies that it has never deliberately pursued a trade surplus and opposes unilateral tariffs (Global Times, [Aug 31]), while the EU wants to convince China to curb exports to the bloc (POLITICO.eu, [Aug 31]). Bilaterally the truce is likely to be extended by one year, with Xi to visit Washington (BigGo Finance, [Aug 28]), even as China opposes the 7.5% tariff plan (Yeni Şafak English, [Aug 27]); the Canada-US trade war is a secondary drag on global trade flows that China aims to win (The Washington Post, [Aug 25]). At home fiscal policy is extracting: a local surtax of 11%–13% has entered legislation (BigGo Finance, [Aug 28]) and The Economist argues Beijing is tightening when it should loosen (The Economist, [Aug 27]).

Markets & Flows: The Hang Seng ended flat at 25,566.99 (BBN Times, [Aug 31]) as China and Hong Kong stocks slipped on weak economic data and the property overhaul (The Economic Times, [Aug 31]). Leadership is defensive: dividend stocks reached an 11-year high at the expense of weak tech (Bloomberg.com, [Aug 31]) and bank stocks are bid, while stock ETFs saw a net outflow of more than 5 billion yuan (36Kr, [Aug 31]).

New / Most Important: The private manufacturing PMI at 51.5 confirms what the official 49.8 only hinted at: the factory pulse turned in August, and it turned on export orders. That is why the PBOC is capping the yuan — a stronger currency would tax the only engine running, with domestic demand still contracting and July loans negative. The policy mix is therefore weak yuan, front-loaded bond issuance and property reform, not rate cuts.

Playbook ✓: China remains a policy-easing outlier in a global hiking environment, and the deflationary-domestic / inflationary-global split it faces is stark: CPI at 0.5% at home against WTI at $89.56 abroad.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Both August PMIs improved just as the trade climate hardened, so the transmission is two-sided. Better new orders and a property package support iron ore demand expectations and the AUD at the margin, but a recovery led by exports, defended by a capped yuan, means more Chinese competition for European exporters facing tougher EU lines, while sub-50 official readings and weak services keep China's import demand soft for EM. The global bond selloff, with the US 10Y at 4.79%, widens the rate differential against the yuan anyway, and war-premium oil is a terms-of-trade tax that eats into the margin gains the PMIs imply.

Macro Stance: Japan is at the epicenter of the global bond repricing. The 10Y JGB yield breached 3% for the first time since 1996. The yen lingers near 160 as Bessent explicitly pressured Japan to boost the yen through rate hikes — an extraordinary public intervention in a sovereign's monetary policy. Japan's Finance Chief pushed back, playing down Bessent's BOJ rate-hike calls.

New / Most Important: This is a structurally NEW development that deserves detailed analysis. Bessent's meeting with Ueda and public statement calling on Japan to hike rates to strengthen the yen represents a fundamental shift in the US-Japan monetary coordination framework. For decades, the US tolerated a weak yen as the price of Japan buying Treasuries. Now Bessent is telling Japan to tighten — which means he's accepting less Japanese Treasury demand in exchange for yen stability. This has enormous implications for the global liquidity cycle: Japan has been the marginal buyer of duration globally, and BOJ hikes + JGB yield normalization will pull capital home from US Treasuries, European bonds, and EM debt. Oxford Economics confirmed "the BoJ will likely hike higher and faster." The 3% JGB yield creates a gravitational pull for the ~$4 trillion in Japanese overseas portfolio investment. If even 10% of that repatriates, it's a $400 billion liquidity drain from global markets. The yen at 160 despite all this hawkish rhetoric shows the market doesn't believe Japan will tighten fast enough — creating asymmetric risk on JPY longs.

Playbook ✓: JGB selloff ↔ global yield surge is the expected transmission mechanism.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Japan's Finance Chief publicly dissenting from Bessent's framing exposes a fault line — the BOJ may move slower than markets now price, creating whipsaw risk in yen crosses.

Macro Stance: The RBA is under pressure to hike in September after unexpectedly high inflation data. Multiple sources confirm hawkish RBA expectations, with commentary noting "Australians just aren't getting the RBA's message" — suggesting the consumption channel of monetary transmission is broken.

New / Most Important: The Australian dollar held firm on hawkish RBA bets, rallying toward the 0.72-0.73 zone. The housing slump is deepening even as the RBA prepares to hike — this is a classic policy dilemma.  |  Playbook ✓: Hot CPI → RBA hike → AUD strength is the standard playbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Hiking into a housing slump is the divergence. The RBA risks triggering a mortgage stress event in a market where household leverage is among the highest globally.

Macro Stance: The day after the inflation surprise, the NBP governor cooled any remaining hopes on rates, saying Poland is entering a period of further structural changes (Interia Biznes, [Sep 1]). The backdrop is yesterday's GUS flash: August CPI at 3.4% y/y and 0.4% m/m (PAP Biznes, [Aug 31]) versus a 3.1% consensus (BIZNES24, [Aug 31]), driven by fuel up 24.2% y/y (CEO Magazyn, [Aug 31]), with mBank now expecting inflation to slightly exceed 4% at year-end (netTG.pl, [Aug 31]). Parkiet's read is that the economy is resilient to the oil shock but inflation is not [Sep 1]. Growth remains the counterweight: Q2 GDP was revised up to 3.9% y/y and 1.0% q/q (PAP Biznes, [Aug 31]) with investment up 8.4% (CEO Magazyn, [Aug 31]) and TVP World calling it an investment surge [Sep 1]; Eurostat put July unemployment at 3.4% (Do Rzeczy, [Sep 1]). The new soft spot is industry: the latest manufacturing PMI fell below the expansion line (Parkiet, [Sep 1]) and Business Insider Polska describes dark clouds and mounting pressure over manufacturing [Sep 1]. Import pass-through (BNY) and divergence against the ECB (ABN AMRO) remain the two-sided squeeze on the zloty, and the euro-area print of 3.3% inflation (Farmer.pl, [Sep 1]) keeps the ECB side of that equation hawkish.

Markets: Orlen's records were not enough: the WIG20 closed down 0.47% on Tuesday (Inwestycje.pl, [Sep 1]) in what Parkiet called a sharp fall [Sep 1], with Grupa Kęty and KGHM the biggest losers (Inwestycje.pl, [Sep 1]), KGHM off more than 3% (Strefa Inwestorów, [Sep 1]) and a correction across state-controlled names (pb.pl, [Sep 1]). Orlen was the exception, up 3.53% (FXMAG, [Sep 1]) and through 160 zł to an all-time high (CrypS.pl, [Sep 1]) as the end of the fuel-price cap lifted pump prices and StockWatch.pl credited geopolitics with lending downstream a hand [Sep 1]. The card, which predates today, already had Orlen at 154.22 (+3.5% 4W), PGE at 11.1 (+8.7% 1W, +6.3% 4W), Dino at 35.98 (+2.7% 1W, +10.8% 4W), Pekao at 259.1 (+5.2% 4W) and PKO BP at 113.96; the laggards are CD Projekt at 234.4 (-8.9% 1W, -7.6% 4W), with FXMAG noting investors rotating from CD Projekt toward KGHM on good long-term forecasts [Sep 1], and EPOL at 44.1 (-0.9% 1W, +2.7% 4W). The zloty is still losing (Comparic.pl, [Sep 1]) with the euro around 4.33 zł (FXMAG, [Sep 1]) and the dollar gaining again (Magazyn MANAGER+, [Sep 1]); the card has USD/PLN at 3.7233 (+1.0% 1W, -0.6% 4W) and EUR/PLN at 4.3273 (+0.5% 1W, +0.4% 4W). POLGBs remain under pressure: the bond sell-off continues and the government is not helping (pb.pl, [Sep 1]), after 10-year yields moved back above 6% (Interia Biznes, [Aug 31]).

Fiscal & Politics: The debt arithmetic took centre stage. Rzeczpospolita reports Poland will borrow less next year but debt will still jump and servicing costs will exceed 100 bn zł [Sep 1]; Parkiet confirms the government is trimming borrowing needs somewhat [Sep 1]. Bankier.pl frames the 7% deficit as a threat of a rating downgrade, with Poland running on a credit of trust [Sep 1], and pb.pl says public debt is balancing on a dangerous line [Sep 1]. The draft itself carries a 282.6 bn zł state deficit, 7.1% of GDP general government and 3% growth in 2027 (Gazeta Prawna, [Aug 28]). Politics turned hotter: Domański attacked President Nawrocki over the end of the CPN programme (Rzeczpospolita, [Sep 1]) and said there is no money in the budget to bring government fuel prices back (Money.pl, [Sep 1]), while the ministry says it will find funds for a permanent US military base (Bankier.pl, [Sep 1]). At the G20 Domański pitched growth, deregulation and investment (pb.pl, [Sep 1]).

Corporate & Sectors: The structural story is in banks: PKO BP becomes the first lender to replace WIBOR with POLSTR in new mortgages from Thursday (Bankier.pl, [Sep 1]), with the rest of the sector given until year-end (pb.pl, [Sep 1]) and Rzeczpospolita warning it does not guarantee cheaper credit [Sep 1]; Simply Wall Street flags Polish banks facing sticky rates with PKO in focus [Sep 1]. PKO BP is also selling covered bonds again (Subiektywnie o finansach, [Sep 1]). PGE surprised the market with net profit above analysts' forecasts (Bankier.pl, [Sep 1]) but, with Polenergia, faces a new government bill on balancing costs (Strefa Inwestorów, [Sep 1]). Orlen froze wholesale prices diplomatically while ARA diesel is the dearest since April (Agro Profil, [Sep 1]) and fuel prices jumped after the cap ended (CEO Magazyn, [Sep 1]). Dino enters ministry-brokered mediation over working conditions on Wednesday (Business Insider Polska, [Sep 1]) even as Investing.com asks whether its correction is over [Sep 1]. CD Projekt reports results with analysts keeping their distance (FXMAG, [Sep 1]). KNF upheld a 20 mln zloty fine on XTB (TradingView, [Sep 1]).

Geopolitics & Security: Putin staged a missile show of force near the NATO border (Ynetnews, [Sep 1]) and the Atlantic Council mapped where he could expand the war beyond Ukraine [Sep 1], days after Tusk said the next seven to eight months are critical (Українська правда, [Aug 29]). Domański said Poland does not trust Russia after its finance minister's US visit (Gazeta Prawna, [Sep 1]); Ukraine eased tensions with Poland over wartime exhumations (Financial Times, [Sep 1]).

New / Most Important: The combination of a contractionary PMI, a 3.4% CPI and a bond sell-off the government is not leaning against is the week's signal: stagflation-lite in industry alongside a central bank that has just told markets not to expect help. Orlen at a record on higher pump prices is the mirror image of the consumer's problem.  |  Playbook ✓: Sticky CEE inflation preventing cuts is consensus; stay long Orlen and PGE on the energy-price tailwind, short duration.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The market is selling KGHM and state names into a growth print of 3.9% and a record investment cycle; if the PMI dip is a European inventory blip rather than a Polish turn, today's correction in cyclicals is a buying opportunity rather than a warning.
Macro Stance: Brazil's economy grew 0.5% in Q2, beating forecasts. As an oil exporter, Brazil is a rare EM beneficiary of the Iran-driven energy price surge.
New / Most Important: The beat on Q2 GDP confirms Brazil's relative resilience.  |  Playbook ✓: Commodity exporter outperformance in a supply-shock regime is textbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None today.
Narrative: The Nasdaq 100 at 29,094 (↓2.1%) is under pressure from rising yields and AI circular-financing fears, while Apple's appointment of John Ternus as CEO marks a generational transition.

Reported: Salesforce rocketed 22% for its second-best day ever, leading a software rally (CNBC, [Aug 27]), after raising FY27 guidance by $300M as Agentforce ARR hit $1.5B (BigGo Finance, [Aug 26]). Intuit is tumbling despite its beat as weak 2027 guidance weighs on the shares (TradingView, [Aug 25]), and HP's drop in PC shipments overshadowed strong revenue growth, sending the shares lower (Reuters, [Aug 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: Dell — goes into its Q2 report as AI server demand soars (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 31]). Palo Alto Networks — Q4 revenue is expected to grow 32% (TradingKey, [Aug 31]) into results due post-market on September 01 (Moomoo, [Aug 26]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Circular financing is the real threat: if hyperscaler capex is partly funded by its own suppliers, it echoes the telecom vendor financing of 1999-2000 that preceded the dot-com bust. Part of the earnings power is financial too — Big Tech profits got a $160bn boost from gains on stakes in other AI companies (Financial Times, [Aug 30]), a line that reverses if AI valuations do.

Narrative: Rising rates compress duration-heavy growth names, and the FTC lawsuit over Amazon's ad practices puts the highest-margin slice of digital advertising under legal threat, while Disney options trading points to elevated single-name volatility.

Reported: Meituan returned to profit as food-delivery competition eased (WSJ, [Aug 28]). JOYY's Q2 revenue rose 16% as AI drove growth across its three core businesses, and it raised full-year profit guidance (BigGo Finance, [Aug 25]). At Nine, subscriber gains at Stan and publishing offset TV ad headwinds (AFR, [Aug 26]).
EPS Upside Watch: Meta — MarketWatch sees a possible 50% rally thanks to an overlooked AI wild card (MarketWatch, [Aug 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: OpenAI's ad business hit a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate (Reuters, [Aug 31]): the AI labs are becoming competitors for the same ad budgets, so the platforms' AI spending may be funding a rival rather than only widening a moat.

Narrative: The curve at +41 bps (little changed over four weeks) is positive but still too flat to be a textbook NIM tailwind, and "Bank of America" and "Morgan Stanley" trending on X without clear catalysts points to news-driven volatility.

Reported: Canada's RBC, TD and CIBC topped profit estimates (Reuters, [Aug 27]), with TD posting the biggest beat of the Big Six as wholesale banking profit soared (Financial Post, [Aug 27]). Affirm's Q4 revenue and GMV topped estimates (Quartz, [Aug 28]).

EPS Upside Watch: TD — RBC sees it positioned for earnings growth and capital returns after a strong Q3 (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 28]), and it is targeting 100 new branch openings in the US (Morningstar, [Aug 27]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The beats came from markets, not margins: TD's wholesale banking net income jumped 87% (Pulse 2.0, [Aug 30]) while RBC's net interest income growth lagged peers (Morningstar, [Aug 27]). With the curve flat and yields rising this fast, mark-to-market losses on bond portfolios — the SVB problem redux — can offset any NIM gain, so trading income is carrying the sector.

Narrative: WTI at $89.56 (↑18.2% vs 4W ago) carries the six-month Iran war premium and US rig counts fell for the first time in six weeks; with China's official factory PMI still below 50 at 49.8, this is a supply shock, not demand pull.

Reported: PetroChina's first-half profit jumped 22% to a record high (OilPrice.com, [Aug 30]), with net profit topping RMB100 billion for the first time and the interim dividend raised 18% (BigGo Finance, [Aug 30]). CNOOC made a record interim profit on higher oil prices and output (Reuters, [Aug 26]). Gazprom's first-half profit fell 12% (Reuters, [Aug 28]).

EPS Upside Watch: Energy Transfer — up 29% in 2026, a run explained by two guidance raises (TIKR.com, [Aug 30]). Venture Global — raised its guidance, a possible signal of a multi-year LNG growth story (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 26]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Supply-driven rallies invite policy responses, and those are arriving: six EU countries are pushing for a windfall tax on oil companies (Yahoo News Singapore, [Aug 29]) and Trump is hosting oil executives after accusing refiners of gouging consumers (Reuters, [Aug 31]) — the war profits are now a political target.
Narrative: Canada-US trade-war headlines and oil-driven input costs squeeze margins, while private equity rolling up small courier firms points to last-mile logistics consolidation.

Reported: Dycom posted an earnings beat tied to AI infrastructure demand (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 27]), but the stock cooled as its backlog became the big question (Simply Wall Street, [Aug 27]). Qantas' profits dipped to a four-year low (The Guardian, [Aug 26]), yet its shares jumped as it unveiled new business-class seats (CNBC, [Aug 27]). Virgin Australia's new planes and fuel hedging shielded it from the oil price shock (SMH.com.au, [Aug 28]).
EPS Upside Watch: IES — sees a data-centre boom and plans a $650M DBM Global acquisition (TradingView, [Aug 27]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The oil shock is sorting airlines by hedge book, not demand: Virgin pays its first dividend since relisting as fuel hedging delivers (AFR, [Aug 28]), while China's 'Big Three' are back in the red as a 'severe' fuel crisis hits earnings (FlightGlobal, [Aug 31]). The cost side, not travel demand, now drives the sector's earnings dispersion.

Narrative: A firearms retailer's Chapter 11 and a 161-year-old kids' clothing chain closing 29 more stores show brick-and-mortar discretionary in secular decline, with rising oil and rates compressing disposable income.

Reported: Dick's Sporting Goods fell 30% as it missed expectations, citing a 'challenging' footwear market (CNBC, [Aug 25]). Best Buy beat quarterly estimates and hiked its outlook, but the stock fell (CNBC, [Aug 27]). Abercrombie's shares rose 36% on a Q2 beat driven by tariff refunds (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 27]).

EPS Upside Watch: Gap — UBS raised its price target to $42 on the earnings outlook (Investing.com UK, [Aug 28]). Lululemon — expected to beat earnings estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 27]), though UBS expects it to cut its fiscal 2026 outlook on weak US and China sales (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail's big Q2 beats came from Washington, not the consumer (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 26]): tariff refunds flatter the prints, and the market pays only when sales grow too — Kohl's fell 6% despite raised guidance and a $150M tariff refund (24/7 Wall St., [Aug 26]). The bear case is about the top line, which refunds cannot fix.
Narrative: Defensive positioning should help staples in a risk-off tape, but oil-driven input-cost inflation erodes margins, leaving the sector split between pricing power and volume pressure.

Reported: Hormel cut its sales outlook amid a consumer pullback and higher costs (WSJ, [Aug 27]) and was the day's worst S&P 500 stock (Barron's, [Aug 27]). J.M. Smucker raised its annual forecast after a strong Q1 beat (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 26]). Dollar General's Q2 sales topped estimates and the stock jumped 12.4% (StockStory, [Aug 27]).
EPS Upside Watch: Indian FMCG makers — a GST cut is lifting volumes and driving a sharp recovery in consumer staples, per BNP Paribas (The Financial Express, [Aug 28]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Dollar stores grow sales as grocers grapple with weak results (Grocery Dive, [Aug 28]), and Dollar Tree attracts higher-income customers as sales climb 7% (PYMNTS.com, [Aug 27]): trade-down is a growth engine for the discount shelf owners, so the margin squeeze is a problem for branded makers like Hormel, not the whole sector.
Narrative: Medtech is the bright spot — Medtronic is flirting with a breakout as its MiniMed spinoff hits a record — and BeOne Medicines' FDA approval marks a turning point per analysts.

Reported: Agilent beat estimates and raised guidance on strong demand, and its shares rose (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 26]). Veeva Systems had its best day ever as the software sector rallied (Barron's, [Aug 27]). Ambu's guidance cut revived old fears (Bloomberg.com, [Aug 26]) after a major stock price drop (MedWatch, [Aug 26]).
EPS Upside Watch: Aveanna — earnings estimates are rising (Yahoo Finance, [Aug 26]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Agilent raised its outlook as China rebounded 9% and pharma reshoring orders began (BigGo Finance, [Aug 26]): part of the defensive sector's new growth is capex — tools makers selling into reshored drug production — which the bond-proxy label misses.

Narrative: Copper is flat (↓0.3%) despite its AI and grid-capex bid while gold surges (↑7.5%) — a hedging bid that is bearish for industrial materials — and China's official factory PMI is still below 50 at 49.8.

Reported: Hochschild Mining jumped as earnings soared on higher gold and silver prices (WSJ, [Aug 26]). Harmony Gold's dividend soared as earnings jumped 87% (MiningMX, [Aug 27]). South32's annual profit jumped 55% and it extended its shareholder-returns program (Mining.com, [Aug 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: Sibanye-Stillwater — earnings are expected to jump 560% (Moneyweb, [Aug 28]) on higher gold and PGM prices (MiningMX, [Aug 27]). Hindustan Zinc — gained 5% after Jefferies raised its target price (NDTV Profit, [Aug 26]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: German chemical industry mood turned positive for the first time in four years, Ifo says (Yahoo! Finance Canada, [Aug 27]): the most energy-sensitive corner of materials is turning up while the sector is priced on a gold-led hedging bid, so the industrial bear case may be late.
Narrative: The 10Y at 4.79% and rising is toxic for rate-sensitive REITs, Australia's housing slump amid RBA hike expectations underscores global vulnerability, and cap rates must decompress further.

Reported: Waypoint REIT posted distributable earnings growth and confirmed its FY26 outlook (The Motley Fool Australia, [Aug 27]), though its shares face mounting pressure from higher interest costs (Simply Wall Street, [Aug 27]). Watkin Jones cut its profit forecast after investor deal delays (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Aug 28]). AEW UK REIT grew portfolio income and kept its 2p quarterly dividend (Yahoo Finance UK, [Aug 26]).
